title: Clinical Integration and Limitations
subtitle: Formulation, consent, outcomes and humility
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating clinical integration and limitations across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain clinical integration and limitations in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in clinical integration and limitations.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to clinical integration and limitations.

sections.explainSimply: EMDR should be integrated into a broader assessment and treatment plan rather than treated as a universal technique.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Use shared decision-making, validated outcomes, risk monitoring, cultural formulation and coordination with other care.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Clinical improvement should be judged by symptoms, functioning and goals—not by presumed neural “processing” or dramatic session experiences.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of clinical integration and limitations as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need clinical integration and limitations to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: A compelling narrative is not a substitute for outcome data.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use clinical integration and limitations to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses clinical integration and limitations to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: A compelling narrative is not a substitute for outcome data. Evidence classification: established clinical governance principles.
